Breaker
brāk´ẽr
n. (one who breaks; in Micah, the One who breaks open the way — Hebrew parats)
From break, Old English brecan. The Hebrew parats means to burst through a wall or a fold — the word used of a breach in a city and of a flock forcing an opening.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Breaker in Micah is a title, and one of the most striking pictures of Christ in the prophets. The chapter has just promised a gathering: “I will surely assemble, O Jacob, all of thee; I will surely gather the remnant of Israel; I will put them together as the sheep of Bozrah, as the flock in the midst of their fold” (Mic 2:12). Then the deliverance: “The breaker is come up before them: they have broken up, and have passed through the gate, and are gone out by it: and their king shall pass before them, and the LORD on the head of them” (Mic 2:13). The image is a penned flock and one who goes up ahead of them and bursts the wall of the fold, so that the sheep pour out through the gap He made, with their king at their head. He goes first; they follow through the opening; the LORD leads them out. Every deliverance of God's people has that shape, and it is finally fulfilled in the One who said, “I am the door: by me if any man enter in, he shall be saved, and shall go in and out, and find pasture” (Joh 10:9). The word has its other, plainer use in Paul: “circumcision verily profiteth, if thou keep the law: but if thou be a breaker of the law, thy circumcision is made uncircumcision” (Rom 2:25).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a breaker as one who breaks; a violator; a transgressor; and also a wave broken by rocks or the shore.

expand to see more

BREAK'ER, n. One who breaks; a violator; a transgressor; as, a breaker of the law.

2. A wave broken by rocks or a sand bank; a surge.

BREACH, n. The act of breaking; a gap or opening made by breaking; as a breach in a wall.

FOLD, n. A pen or inclosure for sheep; a place where a flock of sheep is kept.

Key Scripture

Micah 2:13 — "The breaker is come up before them: they have broken up, and have passed through the gate, and are gone out by it: and their king shall pass before them, and the LORD on the head of them."

Micah 2:12 — "I will surely assemble, O Jacob, all of thee; I will surely gather the remnant of Israel; I will put them together as the sheep of Bozrah, as the flock in the midst of their fold: they shall make great noise by reason of the multitude of men."

John 10:9 — "I am the door: by me if any man enter in, he shall be saved, and shall go in and out, and find pasture."

Romans 2:25 — "For circumcision verily profiteth, if thou keep the law: but if thou be a breaker of the law, thy circumcision is made uncircumcision."

Modern Corruption

Deliverance is expected without a deliverer going first, and religious standing is trusted while the law it belongs to is broken.

expand to see more

Micah 2:13 will not permit a self-help account of salvation. The flock is penned; the wall does not fall on its own; someone goes up before them and bursts it, and only then do they pass through the gate and go out by it. The order in the verse is fixed: the breaker first, the people after, the King at their head. Every scheme in which men break themselves out — by resolve, by ritual, by improvement — has replaced the first clause. And the last clause is worth its own weight: the LORD on the head of them. They do not go out to find their way; they go out behind Him.

Romans 2:25 applies the other sense of the word to the very people who had the covenant sign. Circumcision profits if the law is kept; if a man is a breaker of the law, his circumcision is made uncircumcision. Paul is telling men with the mark that the mark does not hold when the thing it signified is abandoned. The parallel in a Christian congregation is exact and uncomfortable: baptism, membership, attendance and orthodoxy are real and are not nothing, and none of them survives as evidence in a man who lives in settled disobedience. The sign points to a reality; where the reality is absent the sign witnesses against him.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew parats (H6555), to break through, burst out — Micah 2:13, 2 Samuel 5:20 of Baalperazim; porets, the breaker; Greek parabates (G3848), a transgressor — Romans 2:25.

expand to see more

Hebrew parats (H6555) — to break through, make a breach; Micah 2:13, 2 Samuel 5:20, Genesis 38:29 of Pharez.

Hebrew porets — the participle, the breaker; Micah 2:13, used as a title.

Greek parabates (G3848) — a transgressor, one who steps across; Romans 2:25, James 2:11.

The picture is a sheepfold with a wall burst open from the outside, and the flock pouring through the gap.

Micah 2:13 ends with two leaders in one line: their king shall pass before them, and the LORD on the head of them.

Usage

"“The breaker is come up before them” — the wall does not fall on its own."

"“The LORD on the head of them” — they go out behind Him."

"“If thou be a breaker of the law, thy circumcision is made uncircumcision”."
